She always greeted him with a radiantly trusting smile meant just for him, a smile with something more significant in it than the general smile that usually brightened her face. Pierre knew that everyone was waiting for him to say a certain word and cross a certain line, and he knew that sooner or later he would cross it. But an incomprehensible terror seized him at the thought of that dreadful step. A thousand times during that month and a half, feeling himself drawn closer and closer to the terrible precipice, Pierre said to himself: 'What am I doing? I need willpower. Don't I have any?'

He wanted to make a decision, but realized with dismay that in this particular matter he lacked the strength of will that he knew he possessed and had demonstrated before. Pierre was one of those people who are strong only when they feel completely innocent, and ever since that day at Anna Pavlovna's when he was overcome with desire while leaning over the snuffbox, an unacknowledged sense of guilt about that desire had paralyzed his will.

On Helene's name day, a small gathering of 'just family'—as his wife put it—assembled for supper at Prince Vasili's. All these friends and relatives had been given to understand that the young woman's fate would be decided that evening. The guests took their seats at supper. Princess Kuragina, a stout, imposing woman who had once been beautiful, sat at the head of the table. On either side of her were the most important guests—an old general and his wife, and Anna Pavlovna Scherer. At the other end sat the younger and less important guests, along with family members, and there too sat Pierre and Helene, side by side. Prince Vasili wasn't eating supper; he circled the table in high spirits, sitting down with one guest after another and making casual, pleasant remarks to each—except to Pierre and Helene, whose presence he seemed not to notice. He kept the whole party lively. The wax candles burned brightly; the silver and crystal gleamed, as did the ladies' gowns and the gold and silver of the men's epaulettes. Servants in scarlet livery moved around the table; the clatter of plates, knives, and glasses blended with the animated buzz of several conversations. At one end, an old chamberlain was assuring an old baroness of his passionate love for her, at which she laughed. At the other end, someone was telling the story of some poor Mary Viktorovna's misfortunes. In the center, Prince Vasili held everyone's attention. With a playful smile, he was telling the ladies about last Wednesday's meeting of the Imperial Council, at which Sergei Kuzmich Vyazminitov, the new military governor general of Petersburg, had received and read the now-famous letter from Emperor Alexander to Sergei Kuzmich. In it, the Emperor said he was receiving declarations of loyalty from all sides, that the one from Petersburg gave him special pleasure, and that he was proud to lead such a nation and would strive to be worthy of it. The letter began: 'Sergei Kuzmich, From all sides reports reach me...' and so on.
"So he never got past 'Sergei Kuzmich'?" asked one of the ladies.

"Exactly—not one word further," answered Prince Vasili, laughing. "'Sergei Kuzmich... From all sides... From all sides... Sergei Kuzmich...' Poor Vyazminitov couldn't get any further! He would start the letter over and over, but every time he said 'Sergei' he would sob, then 'Kuz-mich'—tears—and 'From all sides' would be swallowed up in sobs, and he couldn't go on. And then the handkerchief again, and again: 'Sergei Kuzmich, From all sides...' and more tears, until finally someone else had to read it."
"Kuzmich... From all sides... and then tears," someone repeated, laughing.
"Don't be cruel," cried Anna Pavlovna from her end of the table, wagging her finger. "He is such a fine, worthy man, our dear Vyazminitov..."

Everyone laughed heartily. At the head of the table, where the honored guests sat, everyone seemed to be in high spirits, excited by many things at once. Only Pierre and Helene sat quietly, almost at the far end, with a suppressed smile on both their faces—a smile that had nothing to do with Sergei Kuzmich, a smile of self-consciousness about their own feelings. But however much the others laughed, talked, joked, and enjoyed their Rhine wine, sauce, and ices, however much they avoided looking at the young couple and seemed oblivious to them, everyone could sense from the occasional glances cast their way that the story about Sergei Kuzmich, the laughter, and the food were all a performance—that the true focus of everyone's attention was Pierre and Helene. Prince Vasili mimicked Sergei Kuzmich's sobbing while glancing at his daughter, and even as he laughed, his expression clearly said: 'Yes... it's moving along, it will all be settled today.' Anna Pavlovna scolded him on behalf of 'our dear Vyazminitov,' but in her eyes, which briefly met Pierre's, Prince Vasili could read congratulations for his future son-in-law and his daughter's happiness. The old princess sighed sadly as she offered wine to the lady beside her and glanced angrily at her daughter, her sigh seeming to say: 'Yes, there's nothing left for you and me but to sip wine, my dear, now that these young ones are being so bold and shamelessly happy.' 'What nonsense I'm thinking!' thought a diplomat, looking at the lovers' happy faces. 'That's happiness!'

Into this trivial, artificial society had entered the simple power of attraction between a healthy, handsome young man and woman. And this human feeling rose above everything else, towering over all their affected chatter. Jokes fell flat, news failed to interest, and the liveliness was clearly forced. Not just the guests but even the servants waiting at table seemed to sense this, forgetting their duties as they gazed at the beautiful Helene with her radiant face and at Pierre's broad, red, happy—though uneasy—face. It was as if the very candlelight focused only on those two happy faces.

Pierre felt that he was at the center of it all, which both pleased and embarrassed him. He was like a man completely absorbed in something. He couldn't see, hear, or understand anything clearly. Only now and then, disconnected ideas and impressions from the real world would flash unexpectedly through his mind.

"So it's all settled!" he thought. "But how did it happen? So quickly! Now I know it's not just because of her or just because of me, but because of everyone—it has to happen. They're all expecting it, they're so certain it will happen that I can't, I simply can't, disappoint them. But how will it turn out? I don't know—but it will definitely happen!" thought Pierre, glancing at those dazzling shoulders so close to his eyes.

Or he would suddenly feel ashamed without knowing why. He felt awkward attracting everyone's attention and being considered a lucky man—him, with his plain face, being seen as some kind of Paris who had won a Helen. 'But it always is this way and has to be!' he reassured himself. 'And besides, what did I do to bring it about? How did it start? I came from Moscow with Prince Vasili. Then nothing happened. So why shouldn't I stay at his house? Then I played cards with her and picked up her handbag and went driving with her. How did it start? When did all this happen?' And here he was sitting beside her as her fiancé, seeing, hearing, and feeling her nearness, her breathing, her movements, her beauty. Then it would suddenly seem that it wasn't she who was so beautiful, but he himself, and that's why everyone was looking at him. Flattered by this general admiration, he would puff out his chest, lift his head, and rejoice in his good fortune. Then suddenly a familiar voice repeated something to him for the second time. But Pierre was so lost in thought that he didn't understand.
"I'm asking when you last heard from Bolkonski," Prince Vasili repeated a third time. "How distracted you are, my dear fellow."

Prince Vasili smiled, and Pierre noticed that everyone was smiling at him and Helene. 'Well, so what if everyone knows?' thought Pierre. 'So what? It's the truth!' And he gave his gentle, childlike smile, and Helene smiled too.
"When did the letter arrive? Was it from Olmütz?" repeated Prince Vasili, pretending he needed to settle a debate.
"How can anyone talk or think about such trivial things?" thought Pierre.
"Yes, from Olmütz," he answered with a sigh.

After supper, Pierre and his partner followed the others into the drawing room. The guests began leaving, some without saying goodbye to Helene. Others came up to her briefly, as if unwilling to distract her from something important, and hurried away, not letting her see them out. The diplomat left the drawing room in mournful silence, reflecting on the pointlessness of his diplomatic career compared to Pierre's happiness. The old general grumbled at his wife when she asked about his leg. 'What an old fool,' he thought. 'That Princess Helene will still be beautiful at fifty.'
"I believe congratulations are in order," Anna Pavlovna whispered to the old princess, kissing her warmly. "If I didn't have this headache, I would have stayed longer."
The old princess didn't reply. She was tormented by jealousy of her daughter's happiness.

While the guests were leaving, Pierre remained alone with Helene for a long time in the small drawing room where they had been sitting. He had often been alone with her during the past six weeks but had never spoken of love. Now he felt it was inevitable, yet he couldn't bring himself to take the final step. He felt ashamed; he felt he was occupying someone else's place beside Helene. 'This happiness is not for you,' some inner voice whispered. 'This happiness is for those who don't have what you have inside you.'
But since he had to say something, he asked if she had enjoyed the party. She replied in her usual simple way that it had been one of the most pleasant name days she could remember.

Some close relatives hadn't left yet and were sitting in the large drawing room. Prince Vasili approached Pierre with slow steps. Pierre stood up and said it was getting late. Prince Vasili gave him a look of stern puzzlement, as if what Pierre had said was too strange to process. But then the severity melted away, and he pulled Pierre's hand down, made him sit, and smiled warmly.

"Well, Lelya?" he said, turning instantly to his daughter with the casual tenderness that parents naturally show children they've spoiled since birth—though Prince Vasili had only learned this manner by imitating other parents.
And he turned back to Pierre.
"Sergei Kuzmich—From all sides—" he said, unbuttoning the top button of his waistcoat.

Pierre smiled, but his smile showed he knew it wasn't the story about Sergei Kuzmich that Prince Vasili was really interested in, and Prince Vasili saw that Pierre knew this. He suddenly mumbled something and walked away. It seemed to Pierre that even the prince was flustered. The sight of this worldly old man's discomfort moved Pierre. He looked at Helene, and she too seemed flustered, her expression seeming to say: 'Well, it's your own fault.'

"The step has to be taken, but I can't, I can't!" thought Pierre, and he started talking about unimportant things again, about Sergei Kuzmich, asking what the point of the story was, since he hadn't heard it properly. Helene smiled and said she had missed it too.
When Prince Vasili returned to the drawing room, his wife, the princess, was whispering to the elderly lady about Pierre.
"Of course it's a brilliant match, but happiness, my dear..."
"Marriages are made in heaven," the elderly lady replied.
Prince Vasili walked past, pretending not to hear them, and sat down on a sofa in a far corner. He closed his eyes as if dozing. His head drooped forward, then he roused himself.
"Aline," he said to his wife, "go see what they're doing."
The princess went to the door, walked past it with a dignified, indifferent air, and peeked into the small drawing room. Pierre and Helene were still sitting and talking, just as before.
"Still the same," she told her husband.

Prince Vasili frowned, his mouth twisting, his cheeks twitching, and his face taking on the coarse, unpleasant expression that was characteristic of him. He shook himself, stood up, threw back his head, and strode purposefully past the ladies into the small drawing room. He walked up to Pierre with quick, joyful steps. His face was so unusually triumphant that Pierre rose in alarm.

"Thank God!" said Prince Vasili. "My wife has told me everything!" He put one arm around Pierre and the other around his daughter. "My dear boy... Lelya... I am so pleased." His voice trembled. "I loved your father... and she will make you a good wife... God bless you!"
He embraced his daughter, then Pierre again, and kissed him. Tears actually wet his cheeks.
"Princess, come here!" he called out.

The old princess came in and wept too. The elderly lady dabbed at her eyes with a handkerchief. Pierre was kissed, and he kissed the beautiful Helene's hand several times. After a while they were left alone again.

"All this had to happen and couldn't have been otherwise," thought Pierre, "so there's no point asking whether it's good or bad. It's good because it's definite, and I'm free of the old tormenting doubt." Pierre held his fiancée's hand in silence, watching her beautiful chest rise and fall.
"Helene!" he said aloud, and paused.
"You're supposed to say something special at a moment like this," he thought, but couldn't remember what people say. He looked at her face. She moved closer. Her face flushed.
"Oh, take those off... those..." she said, pointing at his glasses.

Pierre took them off, and his eyes—besides the strange look that eyes always have right after glasses are removed—also had a frightened, questioning expression. He was about to lean over and kiss her hand, but with a quick, almost rough movement, she intercepted his lips with her own. Her face, with its altered, unpleasantly excited expression, startled Pierre.
"It's too late now, it's done. Besides, I love her," thought Pierre.
"I love you!" he said (in French), remembering what you're supposed to say at such moments. But his words sounded so feeble that he felt embarrassed.
* Je vous aime!
Six weeks later he was married and settled in Count Bezukhov's large, newly furnished Petersburg house—the happy owner, as everyone said, of a beautiful, celebrated wife and millions of rubles.

chapters.title: Book Three (1805) — Chapter 3
paragraphs: Old Prince Nicholas Bolkonski received a letter from Prince Vasili in November 1805, announcing that he and his son would be visiting. 'I'm going on an inspection tour, and of course I won't mind an extra seventy miles to see you, my esteemed benefactor,' wrote Prince Vasili. 'My son Anatole is traveling with me on his way to the army, so I hope you'll allow him to personally express the deep respect that, following his father's example, he feels for you.'
"It seems we won't need to introduce Mary to society—suitors are coming to us on their own," the little princess carelessly remarked upon hearing the news.
Prince Bolkonski frowned but said nothing.
Two weeks after the letter, Prince Vasili's servants arrived one evening ahead of him, and he and his son came the next day.

Old Bolkonski had always had a low opinion of Prince Vasili's character, and even more so recently, since under Paul and Alexander, Prince Vasili had risen to high positions and honors. Now, from the hints in his letter and from the little princess's comments, he saw where this was heading, and his low opinion turned to contemptuous hostility. He snorted whenever Prince Vasili's name came up. On the day of the visit, the old prince was especially irritable and out of sorts. Whether he was in a bad mood because Prince Vasili was coming, or whether his bad mood made the visit especially annoying, he was difficult. That morning, Tikhon had already warned the architect not to go to the prince with his report.
"Hear how he's walking?" said Tikhon, drawing the architect's attention to the sound of the prince's footsteps. "Flat on his heels—we know what that means..."

Still, at nine o'clock, the prince put on his velvet coat with a sable collar and cap and went out for his usual walk. It had snowed the day before, and the path to the greenhouse that the prince always took had been swept clean. The marks of the broom were still visible in the snow, and a shovel had been left stuck in one of the snowbanks lining both sides of the path. The prince walked through the conservatories, the servants' quarters, and the outbuildings, frowning and silent.
"Can a sleigh get through?" he asked his steward, a dignified man who resembled his master in manner and appearance, as they walked back toward the house.
"The snow is deep. I'm having the drive swept, your honor."
The prince nodded and went up to the porch. 'Thank God,' thought the steward, 'the storm has passed!'
"It would have been hard to drive up, your honor," the steward added. "I heard that a minister is coming to visit, your honor."
The prince spun around and fixed his eyes on the steward, frowning.

"What? A minister? What minister? Who gave those orders?" he snapped in his shrill, harsh voice. "The road isn't swept for my daughter the princess, but for a minister! For me, there are no ministers!"
"Your honor, I thought—"

"You thought!" the prince shouted, his words coming faster and more garbled. "You thought!... Scoundrels! Idiots!... I'll teach you to think!" And he raised his walking stick and would have struck Alpatych, the steward, if the man hadn't instinctively jumped back. "Thought... Idiots..." the prince shouted.

But although Alpatych, frightened by his own boldness in dodging the blow, stepped forward with his bald head bowed submissively—or perhaps for that very reason—the prince, though he kept shouting "Idiots! Throw the snow back on the road!" didn't raise his stick again and hurried into the house.

Before dinner, Princess Mary and Mademoiselle Bourienne, who knew the prince was in a bad mood, stood waiting for him. Mademoiselle Bourienne had a bright expression that said, 'I know nothing, I'm the same as always,' while Princess Mary was pale, frightened, with downcast eyes. What she found hardest to bear was knowing that at times like these she should act like Mademoiselle Bourienne, but couldn't. She thought: 'If I act as if nothing's wrong, he'll think I don't care. But if I look sad and gloomy, he'll say—as he has before—that I'm sulking.'
The prince looked at his daughter's frightened face and snorted.
"Fool... or dunce!" he muttered.
"And the other one isn't here either. They've been gossiping," he thought, referring to the little princess, who wasn't in the dining room.
"Where is the princess?" he asked. "Hiding?"
"She isn't feeling well," Mademoiselle Bourienne answered with a bright smile. "She won't be coming down. It's natural in her condition."
"Hm! Hm!" the prince muttered, sitting down.

His plate seemed not quite clean to him. Pointing at a spot, he flung it away. Tikhon caught it and passed it to a footman. The little princess wasn't actually ill, but she was so terrified of the prince that, hearing he was in a bad temper, she had decided not to come down.
"I'm worried about the baby," she told Mademoiselle Bourienne. "Who knows what a fright could do."

In general, life at Bald Hills meant constant fear for the little princess, mixed with a feeling of dislike for the old prince that she didn't acknowledge because the fear was so much stronger. The prince returned that dislike, but it was overwhelmed by his contempt for her. Once the little princess had settled in at Bald Hills, she took a particular liking to Mademoiselle Bourienne, spent whole days with her, asked her to sleep in her room, and often talked with her about the old prince, criticizing him.

"So we're going to have visitors, Prince?" said Mademoiselle Bourienne, unfolding her white napkin with her pink fingers. "His Excellency Prince Vasili Kuragin and his son, I understand?" she said, as if asking for confirmation.

"Hm—his excellency is a lightweight... I got him his position," the prince said dismissively. "Why his son is coming, I have no idea. Maybe Princess Elizabeth and Princess Mary know. I don't want him." He looked at his blushing daughter. "Are you unwell today? Eh? Scared of the 'minister,' as that fool Alpatych called him this morning?"
"No, Father."

Although Mademoiselle Bourienne had chosen her topic poorly, she didn't stop talking. She chattered about the conservatories and a flower that had just bloomed. After the soup, the prince became more pleasant.
After dinner he went to visit his daughter-in-law. The little princess was sitting at a small table chatting with Masha, her maid. She turned pale when she saw her father-in-law.
She had changed a great deal. She was now plain rather than pretty. Her cheeks had hollowed, her lip curled up, and her eyes were drawn down.
"Yes, I feel some pressure," she said in answer to the prince's question about how she was feeling.
"Do you need anything?"
"No, thank you, Father."
"Very well then."
He left the room and went to the vestibule, where Alpatych stood with his head bowed.
"Was the snow put back?"
"Yes, your excellency. Forgive me, for heaven's sake... It was just my stupidity."
"Fine, fine," the prince interrupted, and with his strange, forced laugh, he held out his hand for Alpatych to kiss, then went to his study.

Prince Vasili arrived that evening. He was met on the drive by coachmen and servants who, shouting loudly, dragged his sleighs up to one of the lodges over the road that had been deliberately piled with snow.
Prince Vasili and Anatole were given separate rooms.

Anatole, having taken off his coat, sat with arms crossed before a table, smilingly and absent-mindedly fixing his large, handsome eyes on one corner. He viewed his entire life as one continuous round of entertainment that someone, for some reason, had to provide for him. He regarded this visit to a grumpy old man and a rich, ugly heiress the same way. It might all turn out quite nicely and amusingly. 'And why not marry her if she really has that much money? That never hurts,' thought Anatole.

He shaved and perfumed himself with the care and elegance that had become second nature, and with his handsome head held high, entered his father's room with his naturally cheerful and confident air. Prince Vasili's two valets were busy dressing him. He looked around with great animation and gave his son a friendly nod as he entered, as if to say: 'Yes, that's exactly how I want you to look.'
"Seriously though, Father, is she really that ugly?" Anatole asked, as if picking up a conversation they'd had many times on the journey.
"Enough! Don't be ridiculous! Above all, try to be respectful and careful with the old prince."
"If he starts making trouble, I'm leaving," said Anatole. "I can't stand those old men! Right?"
"Remember, everything depends on this for you."

Meanwhile, it wasn't just the servants who knew the minister and his son had arrived—both their appearances had been described in minute detail. Princess Mary sat alone in her room, trying in vain to calm her anxiety.

"Why did they write? Why did Lise tell me about it? It can never happen!" she said, looking at herself in the mirror. "How will I walk into the drawing room? Even if I like him, I can't be myself with him now." The mere thought of her father's look filled her with dread. The little princess and Mademoiselle Bourienne had already received from Masha, the lady's maid, a thorough report on how handsome the minister's son was, with his rosy cheeks and dark eyebrows, and how his father had barely managed to drag his legs upstairs while the son had bounded up like an eagle, three steps at a time. With this intelligence in hand, the little princess and Mademoiselle Bourienne, whose chattering voices had been audible from the hallway, went into Princess Mary's room.
"Did you know they've arrived, Marie?" said the little princess, waddling in and sinking heavily into an armchair.

She had changed out of her usual loose morning gown and put on one of her best dresses. Her hair was done up and her face was lively—though this couldn't hide how much thinner and paler she had become. Dressed as she used to be in Petersburg society, it was even more obvious how much plainer she looked now. Some subtle touch had been added to Mademoiselle Bourienne's outfit that made her fresh, pretty face even more appealing.

"What—are you going to stay like that, dear princess?" she began. "They're going to announce the gentlemen in the drawing room any minute and we'll have to go down, and you haven't done anything with yourself!"

The little princess jumped up, rang for the maid, and with cheerful energy began planning how to dress Princess Mary. Princess Mary's pride was wounded by the fact that a suitor's arrival excited her, and even more by her companions' complete inability to imagine she might feel differently about it. To tell them she was embarrassed—for herself and for them—would be to reveal her agitation. To refuse their help would only prolong their teasing and insistence. She blushed, her beautiful eyes dimmed, red blotches appeared on her face, and it took on the unattractive, long-suffering expression it so often wore as she submitted to Mademoiselle Bourienne and Lise. Both women sincerely tried to make her pretty. She was so plain that neither could see her as a rival, so they set about dressing her with genuine conviction—the unshakable female belief that clothes can make any face pretty.

"No, really, dear, this dress won't do," said Lise, studying Princess Mary from a distance. "You have a maroon dress—go get it. Seriously! Your whole life might depend on this. But this one is too light, it's not right for you!"

It wasn't the dress but Princess Mary's face and whole figure that weren't attractive. But neither Mademoiselle Bourienne nor the little princess could see this. They still believed that if a blue ribbon were placed in her hair, the hair pinned up, and the blue scarf lowered on the best maroon dress, everything would be fine. They forgot that the anxious face and the figure couldn't be changed, and that no matter how much they altered the setting and accessories around that face, it would still look sad and plain. After two or three outfit changes—to which Princess Mary meekly submitted—once her hair had been piled on top of her head (a style that completely altered and worsened her appearance) and she had put on a maroon dress with a pale-blue scarf, the little princess circled her twice, adjusting a fold here, straightening the scarf there, tilting her head this way and that.

"No, it won't work," she said firmly, clasping her hands. "No, Marie, this dress really doesn't suit you. I prefer you in your little gray everyday dress. Please, do it for my sake. Katie," she called to the maid, "bring the princess her gray dress, and you'll see, Mademoiselle Bourienne, how I'll fix it up." She smiled with the anticipated pleasure of an artist.

But when Katie brought the gray dress, Princess Mary sat motionless before the mirror, staring at her face. In the reflection she could see her eyes filling with tears and her mouth quivering, about to burst into sobs.
"Come, dear princess," said Mademoiselle Bourienne, "just one more little effort."
The little princess took the dress from the maid and came over to Princess Mary.
"Now we'll make something simple and flattering," she said.
The three voices—hers, Mademoiselle Bourienne's, and Katie's, who was laughing at something—blended together in a cheerful sound, like birdsong.
"No, leave me alone," said Princess Mary.

Her voice sounded so serious and so sad that the birdsong stopped at once. They looked at her beautiful, large, thoughtful eyes, shining with tears and unspoken thoughts, gazing imploringly at them—and understood that insisting would be useless, even cruel.

"At least change your hairstyle," said the little princess. "Didn't I tell you," she added, turning reproachfully to Mademoiselle Bourienne, "that Mary's face doesn't suit that style at all? Not at all! Please change it."
"Leave me alone, please leave me alone! It's all the same to me," answered a voice struggling with tears.

Mademoiselle Bourienne and the little princess had to admit to themselves that Princess Mary looked very plain like this—worse than usual—but it was too late. She gazed at them with an expression they both knew well: thoughtful and sad. This look never frightened anyone (she was never intimidating), but they knew that when it appeared, she became silent and nothing could change her mind.
"You will change it, won't you?" said Lise. When Princess Mary didn't answer, she left the room.

Princess Mary was left alone. She didn't do as Lise asked; she not only kept her hair as it was but didn't even glance in the mirror. Letting her arms fall helplessly, she sat with downcast eyes and lost herself in thought. In her imagination, a husband appeared—a man, strong, commanding, and strangely attractive—and carried her away into a completely different, happy world. She imagined a child, her own—like the one she had seen yesterday in her nurse's daughter's arms—at her breast, with the husband standing beside her, gazing tenderly at her and the baby. 'But no, it's impossible—I'm too ugly,' she thought.
"Please come to tea. The prince will be out in a moment," came the maid's voice from the door.

She stirred and was appalled at what she had been thinking. Before going downstairs, she went into the room where the icons hung and stood before the dark face of a large icon of the Savior, lit by a lamp, her hands folded in prayer. A painful doubt filled her soul. Could the joy of love—earthly love for a man—really be meant for her? In her dreams of marriage, Princess Mary imagined happiness and children, but her deepest, most hidden longing was for earthly love. The harder she tried to conceal this feeling from others and from herself, the stronger it grew. 'Oh God,' she said, 'how can I overcome these temptations? How can I give up these sinful dreams and peacefully fulfill Your will?' And as soon as she asked the question, God answered in her own heart. 'Desire nothing for yourself. Seek nothing. Be not anxious or envious. The future—both mankind's and your own—must remain hidden from you. But live so that you are ready for anything. If God wills that you be tested in marriage, be ready to fulfill His will.' With this comforting thought—though still harboring hope for the fulfillment of her forbidden earthly longing—Princess Mary sighed, crossed herself, and went downstairs, thinking not of her dress or hairstyle or how she would enter or what she would say. What did any of that matter compared to the will of God, without whose care not a single hair falls from anyone's head?

chapters.title: Book Three (1805) — Chapter 4
paragraphs: When Princess Mary came downstairs, Prince Vasili and his son were already in the drawing room, talking with the little princess and Mademoiselle Bourienne. As she entered with her heavy step, walking on her heels, the gentlemen and Mademoiselle Bourienne stood up, and the little princess pointed her out to the guests: 'Here's Marie!' Princess Mary saw them all and registered every detail. She saw Prince Vasili's face go serious for an instant when he noticed her, then immediately break into a smile again. She saw the little princess watching curiously for the impression 'Marie' would make. She saw Mademoiselle Bourienne with her ribbon and pretty face, looking unusually animated, her eyes fixed on him. But him she couldn't really see—she only saw something large, brilliant, and handsome moving toward her. Prince Vasili approached first, and she kissed the bold forehead that bent over her hand, answering his question by saying that she remembered him perfectly well. Then Anatole came up. She still couldn't see him clearly. She only felt a soft hand take hers firmly, and her lips touched a white forehead framed by beautiful light-brown hair that smelled of pomade. When she finally looked up, she was struck by his beauty. Anatole stood with his right thumb hooked under a button of his uniform, his chest out, his back straight, gently shifting his weight on one foot, his head tilted slightly, looking at the princess with a beaming face—not speaking and obviously not thinking about her at all. Anatole wasn't quick-witted or eloquent in conversation, but he had the invaluable social gift of composure and unshakable self-assurance. If a man who lacks confidence stays silent at a first meeting, betraying awareness of the awkwardness and anxiety to fill it, the effect is bad. But Anatole was silent, he shifted his weight, and he smiled while studying the princess's hair arrangement. He clearly could have stayed silent like this for a very long time. 'If anyone finds this silence uncomfortable, they can talk, but I don't feel like it,' he seemed to say. Beyond this, in his manner with women, Anatole had a way that particularly inspired curiosity, awe, and even love—a casual awareness of his own superiority. It was as though he were saying to them: 'I know you. I know you very well. But why should I bother with you? You'd be delighted, of course.' Perhaps he didn't actually think this when meeting women—most likely he didn't, since he rarely thought much at all—but his looks and behavior gave that impression. The princess sensed it, and as if wanting to show that she didn't even expect to interest him, she turned to his father. The conversation was lively and animated, thanks to Princess Lise's voice and her little downy lip curving over her white teeth. She greeted Prince Vasili with the playful manner common to chatty, lively people—the kind that assumes a shared history of private jokes and fond memories between speaker and listener, even when no such history exists. Prince Vasili played along easily, and the little princess also drew Anatole, whom she barely knew, into these entertaining recollections of things that had never happened. Mademoiselle Bourienne joined in too, and even Princess Mary felt herself pleasantly pulled into these cheerful, fictional reminiscences.

"Here at least we'll have you all to ourselves, dear prince," the little princess said to Prince Vasili in French. "It's not like at Annette's parties, where you always ran off. You remember dear Annette!"
(Anna Pavlovna.)
"Oh, but you won't lecture me about politics like Annette!"
"And our little tea table?"
"Oh, yes!"

"Why were you never at Annette's?" the little princess asked Anatole. "Oh, I know, I know," she said with a sly look, "your brother Hippolyte told me all about your adventures. Oh!" And she wagged her finger at him. "I've even heard about your escapades in Paris!"

"And didn't Hippolyte tell you," asked Prince Vasili, turning to his son and grabbing the little princess's arm as if she were about to escape, "how he pined for the dear princess, and how she showed him the door? Oh, she's a pearl among women, princess," he added, turning to Princess Mary.
When Paris was mentioned, Mademoiselle Bourienne seized the chance to join in.

She asked if it had been long since Anatole left Paris and whether he had enjoyed it there. Anatole answered the Frenchwoman readily and, studying her with a smile, chatted with her about her homeland. When he noticed the pretty little Bourienne, Anatole decided that life at Bald Hills might not be boring after all. 'Not bad at all!' he thought (in French), looking her over. 'Not bad at all, that little companion! Hopefully she'll come along when we're married. She's quite charming.'
* la petite est gentille

The old prince took his time dressing in his study, frowning and thinking about what to do. These visitors annoyed him. 'What are Prince Vasili and that son of his to me? Prince Vasili is a shallow braggart, and his son is probably a fine specimen,' he grumbled to himself. What really angered him was that the visit forced him to face a question he always tried to suppress, one about which he was always dishonest with himself: could he ever bring himself to give up his daughter and let her marry? The prince never asked himself the question directly, knowing he would have to answer it honestly, and honesty clashed not just with his feelings but with the very possibility of his life. Life without Princess Mary—little as he seemed to value her—was unthinkable to him. 'Why should she marry?' he thought. 'To be miserable, that's certain. Look at Lise, married to Andrew—you'd think a better husband couldn't be found these days—but is she happy? And who would marry Mary for love? She's plain and awkward! They'd only want her for her connections and money. There are plenty of women living unmarried, and they're happier for it.' So thought Prince Bolkonski while dressing. Yet the question he kept putting off demanded an immediate answer. Prince Vasili had brought his son with the obvious intention of proposing, and today or tomorrow he would likely expect an answer. His birth and social position were acceptable. 'Well, I have nothing against it,' the prince said to himself, 'but he has to be worthy of her. And that's what we'll find out.'
"That's what we'll see! That's what we'll see!" he said aloud.

He entered the drawing room with his usual brisk step, glancing quickly around the room. He noticed the little princess's change of dress, Mademoiselle Bourienne's ribbon, Princess Mary's unflattering hairstyle, Mademoiselle Bourienne's and Anatole's smiles, and his daughter's loneliness amid the general conversation. 'Dressed herself up like a fool!' he thought irritably, looking at her. 'No shame! And he ignores her!'
He went straight up to Prince Vasili.
"Well! Hello! Hello! Good to see you!"
"Friendship laughs at distance," Prince Vasili began in his usual rapid, confident, familiar tone. "Here is my second son. Please be kind to him."
Prince Bolkonski studied Anatole.
"Fine young man! Fine young man!" he said. "Well, come give me a kiss." And he offered his cheek.
Anatole kissed the old man and studied him with curiosity and perfect composure, waiting for the eccentric behavior his father had warned him about.

Prince Bolkonski sat down in his usual corner of the sofa and, pulling up an armchair for Prince Vasili, gestured for him to sit. He began asking about politics and the news, seeming to listen carefully to what Prince Vasili said while constantly glancing at Princess Mary.
"So they're writing from Potsdam already?" he said, repeating Prince Vasili's last words. Then he suddenly got up and walked over to his daughter.

"Is that how you dress for visitors, eh?" he said. "Very nice, very nice! You've done your hair in a new way for the guests, and in front of the guests I'm telling you: never again dare change your appearance without my permission."
"It was my fault, Father," the little princess interjected, blushing.
"You may do as you please," Prince Bolkonski told his daughter-in-law with a bow, "but she doesn't need to make herself look ridiculous—she's plain enough as it is."
And he sat down again, paying no more attention to his daughter, who was in tears.
"On the contrary, that hairstyle suits the princess very well," said Prince Vasili.
"Now then, young prince—what's your name?" said Prince Bolkonski, turning to Anatole. "Come here, let's talk and get to know each other."
"Now the fun begins," thought Anatole, sitting down beside the old prince with a smile.

"Well, my boy, I hear you were educated abroad—not taught to read by the village deacon, like your father and me. Tell me, are you serving in the Horse Guards?" asked the old man, scrutinizing Anatole closely.
"No, I've been transferred to a line regiment," said Anatole, barely suppressing a laugh.
"Ah! Good thing. So, my boy, you want to serve the Tsar and the country? It's wartime. A fine fellow like you should serve. Well, are you heading to the front?"
"No, Prince, our regiment has moved to the front, but I'm attached... what am I attached to, Papa?" said Anatole, turning to his father with a laugh.
"Splendid soldier, splendid! 'What am I attached to!' Ha, ha, ha!" laughed Prince Bolkonski, and Anatole laughed even harder. Suddenly the old prince frowned.
"You may go," he told Anatole.
Anatole returned to the ladies with a smile.
"So you had him educated abroad, Prince Vasili?" said the old prince.
"I did my best for him, and I can assure you the education there is much better than ours."

"Yes, everything is different nowadays, everything has changed. The boy's a fine fellow, a fine fellow! Well, come with me." He took Prince Vasili by the arm and led him to his study. As soon as they were alone, Prince Vasili laid out his hopes and intentions.

"What, do you think I'd stop her? That I can't bear to part with her?" the old prince said angrily. "What an idea! I'm ready tomorrow! Only let me tell you, I want to know my future son-in-law better. You know my principles—everything in the open! I'll ask her tomorrow, with you there. If she's willing, then he can stay. He can stay and I'll observe him." He snorted. "Let her marry—it's all the same to me!" he shouted in the same piercing voice he had used when saying goodbye to his son.

"I'll be frank with you," said Prince Vasili, in the tone of a cunning man who has decided there's no point being cunning with someone so sharp. "You know people, you see right through them. Anatole is no genius, but he's an honest, good-hearted young man—an excellent son and kinsman."
"Fine, fine, we'll see!"

As always happens when women live alone for a long time without male company, the arrival of Anatole made all three women of Prince Bolkonski's household feel that their lives up to that point hadn't been real. Their powers of thinking, feeling, and observing increased tenfold, and their existence, which seemed to have been spent in darkness, was suddenly filled with new, meaningful light.

Princess Mary became completely oblivious to her face and hair. The open, handsome face of the man who might become her husband consumed all her attention. He seemed to her kind, brave, determined, manly, and generous. She felt certain of it. Thousands of dreams about family life rose endlessly in her imagination. She tried to push them away and hide them.

"But am I being too cold with him?" the princess wondered. "I'm trying to hold back because deep down I already feel too close to him. But he can't know what I'm thinking and might believe I don't like him."
And Princess Mary tried—but couldn't manage—to be warm to her new guest. 'Poor girl, she's hopelessly ugly!' thought Anatole.

Mademoiselle Bourienne, also stirred by Anatole's arrival, had quite different thoughts. A beautiful young woman with no real status, no family, not even a country of her own, she certainly hadn't intended to devote her life to serving Prince Bolkonski, reading aloud to him, and being Princess Mary's companion. Mademoiselle Bourienne had long been waiting for a Russian prince who would recognize at a glance her superiority over the plain, badly dressed, ungainly Russian princesses, fall in love with her, and carry her away. And here at last was a Russian prince. She had a story, heard from her aunt but embellished in her own imagination, that she loved to replay in her mind. It was about a girl who had been seduced, and whose poor mother appeared to reproach her for giving herself to a man without marriage. Mademoiselle Bourienne was often moved to tears as she imagined telling this story to him, her seducer. And now he, a real Russian prince, had appeared. He would carry her off, and then her poor mother would appear, and he would marry her. So her future took shape in Mademoiselle Bourienne's mind even as she chatted with Anatole about Paris. It wasn't calculation guiding her—she didn't even stop to think about what she should do—but all of this had been familiar to her for so long that now, with Anatole present, it simply arranged itself around him, and she wished and tried to please him as much as possible.

The little princess, like a retired warhorse hearing the trumpet, unconsciously and completely forgetting her condition, prepared for the familiar thrill of flirtation—without ulterior motive or inner struggle, with simple, lighthearted pleasure.

Although Anatole usually played the role of a man weary of being chased by women, his vanity was flattered by the sight of his power over these three women. Besides that, he was beginning to feel for the pretty, provocative Mademoiselle Bourienne that passionate, animal desire that tended to seize him suddenly and drive him to the most reckless behavior.

After tea, the group moved to the sitting room and Princess Mary was asked to play the clavichord. Anatole, laughing and in high spirits, leaned on his elbows facing her, next to Mademoiselle Bourienne. Princess Mary felt his gaze with a painful, joyful emotion. Her favorite sonata carried her into a deeply poetic inner world, and the look she felt on her made that world even more beautiful. But Anatole's eyes, though aimed at her, were actually focused on Mademoiselle Bourienne's little foot, which he was nudging with his own under the clavichord. Mademoiselle Bourienne was looking at Princess Mary too, and in her lovely eyes there was an expression of fearful excitement and hope that was new to the princess.

"How she loves me!" thought Princess Mary. "How happy I am now, and how happy I could be with such a friend and such a husband! A husband? Is it really possible?" she thought, not daring to look at his face but still feeling his eyes on her.

That evening, after supper, as everyone was about to retire, Anatole kissed Princess Mary's hand. She didn't know where she found the courage, but she looked straight into his handsome face as it came close to her nearsighted eyes. After Princess Mary, he went up and kissed Mademoiselle Bourienne's hand. (This wasn't proper etiquette, but he did everything with such easy confidence!) Mademoiselle Bourienne blushed and gave the princess a frightened glance.

"What sensitivity!" thought the princess. "Is it possible that Amélie"—Mademoiselle Bourienne—"thinks I could be jealous of her and fail to appreciate her pure devotion to me?" She went over and warmly kissed her. Anatole then went to kiss the little princess's hand.
"No! No! No! When your father writes to tell me you've been behaving yourself, I'll let you kiss my hand. Not before!" she said. And with a teasing smile, wagging her finger, she left the room.

chapters.title: Book Three (1805) — Chapter 5
paragraphs: They all went their separate ways, but except for Anatole, who fell asleep the moment he hit the pillow, everyone lay awake for a long time that night.

"Is he really going to be my husband, this stranger who is so kind — yes, kind, that's the most important thing," thought Princess Mary. Then a fear she rarely experienced came over her. She was afraid to look behind her — it felt as though someone was standing there behind the screen in the dark corner. And that someone was the devil — and he was also this man with the white forehead, black eyebrows, and red lips.
She rang for her maid and asked her to sleep in her room.

Mademoiselle Bourienne paced the conservatory for a long time that evening, waiting in vain for someone, alternately smiling at imaginary encounters and working herself up to tears with the imagined words of her poor mother scolding her for her moral downfall.

The little princess complained to her maid that the bed was badly made. She couldn't get comfortable lying on her stomach or on her side. Every position felt awkward and unbearable, and the weight of her pregnancy bothered her more than ever because Anatole's presence had vividly reminded her of the time when she wasn't like this, when everything was light and carefree. She sat in an armchair in her dressing jacket and nightcap while Katie, sleepy and disheveled, beat and turned the heavy feather mattress for the third time, muttering to herself.
"I told you it was all lumps and holes!" the little princess repeated. "I'd love to fall asleep — it's not my fault!" Her voice quivered like a child about to cry.

The old prince couldn't sleep either. Tikhon, half asleep, heard him pacing angrily and snorting. The old prince felt as if he'd been insulted through his daughter. The insult stung all the more because it wasn't directed at him personally, but at his daughter, whom he loved more than himself. He kept telling himself he would think the whole matter through carefully and decide what was right, but instead he only got more and more worked up.

"The first man who comes along — she forgets her father and everything else, runs upstairs and does her hair and wags her tail and becomes a different person! Happy to throw her father over! And she knew I'd notice. Hmph... hmph... hmph! And can't I see that idiot only had eyes for Bourienne — I'll have to get rid of her. And how is it she doesn't have enough pride to see it? If she has no pride for her own sake, she should at least have some for mine! She needs to be shown that this fool thinks nothing of her and only looks at Bourienne. No, she has no pride... but I'll show her..."

The old prince knew that if he told his daughter she was mistaken, that Anatole was really interested in Mademoiselle Bourienne, it would wound Princess Mary's self-esteem, and his own goal — not to be separated from her — would be achieved. Calming himself with this thought, he called Tikhon and began to undress.

"What the devil brought them here?" he thought, while Tikhon pulled the nightshirt over his dried-up old body and gray-haired chest. "I never invited them. They came to disrupt my life — and there isn't much of it left."
"Devil take them!" he muttered while his head was still covered by the shirt.
Tikhon knew his master's habit of sometimes thinking aloud, so he met the angry, questioning expression on the face that emerged from the shirt with an unchanged look.
"Have they gone to bed?" the prince asked.
Tikhon, like all good valets, instinctively sensed the direction of his master's thoughts. He guessed the question was about Prince Vasili and his son.
"They've retired and put out their lights, your excellency."
"No good... no good..." the prince said quickly, and thrusting his feet into his slippers and his arms into his dressing gown, he went to the couch where he slept.

Although no words had passed between Anatole and Mademoiselle Bourienne, they understood each other perfectly regarding the first act of their romance, up to the appearance of the poor mother. They understood they had much to say to each other in private and had been looking for a chance to meet alone since morning. When Princess Mary went to her father's room at the usual hour, Mademoiselle Bourienne and Anatole met in the conservatory.

Princess Mary approached the door of the study with particular dread. It seemed to her that not only did everyone know her fate would be decided that day, but that they also knew what she thought about it. She read this in Tikhon's face and in the face of Prince Vasili's valet, who gave her a deep bow when she passed him in the corridor carrying hot water.

The old prince was unusually gentle and attentive in his treatment of his daughter that morning. Princess Mary knew this painstaking manner well. His face wore that expression when his dry hands clenched in frustration at her not understanding an arithmetic problem, when he would get up from his chair and walk away, repeating the same words in a low voice several times.
He came straight to the point, treating her with a forced formality.

"I've received a proposal concerning you," he said with an unnatural smile. "I expect you've guessed that Prince Vasili didn't come here and bring his pupil" — for some reason Prince Bolkonski referred to Anatole as a 'pupil' — "just to admire my beautiful eyes. Last night a proposal was made on your behalf, and as you know my principles, I'm leaving the decision to you."
"How should I understand you, Father?" said the princess, growing pale and then blushing.

"What do you mean, how?" her father cried angrily. "Prince Vasili has taken a liking to you as a daughter-in-law and is proposing on his pupil's behalf. That's what there is to understand! 'How should I understand?' ... I'm the one asking you!"
"I don't know what you think, Father," the princess whispered.
"Me? What about me? Leave me out of this. I'm not the one getting married. What about you? That's what I want to know."

The princess could see that her father disapproved, but at that moment the thought struck her that her fate would be decided now or never. She lowered her eyes to avoid his gaze, under which she felt she could only submit out of habit rather than think clearly, and said: "I only want to do your will, but if I had to express my own wish..." She didn't have time to finish. The old prince cut her off.
"Wonderful!" he shouted. "He'll take you with your dowry and grab Mademoiselle Bourienne as a bonus. She'll be the real wife, while you..."
The prince stopped. He saw the effect his words had on his daughter. She lowered her head and was about to burst into tears.

"Now then, now then — I'm only joking!" he said. "Remember this, Princess: I believe firmly that a young woman has every right to choose. I'm giving you complete freedom. Just remember that your life's happiness depends on your decision. Don't worry about me!"
"But I don't know, Father!"

"There's no need for discussion! He takes orders and will marry you or anyone else. But you are free to choose... Go to your room, think it over, and come back in an hour to tell me in his presence: yes or no. I know you'll pray about it. Fine, pray if you want, but you'd better think it over too. Go! Yes or no, yes or no, yes or no!" he kept shouting even as the princess, as if lost in a fog, had already stumbled out of the study.

Her fate was decided, and happily decided. But what her father had said about Mademoiselle Bourienne was terrible. It couldn't be true, of course, but still it was awful, and she couldn't stop thinking about it. She was walking straight through the conservatory, not seeing or hearing anything, when suddenly the familiar whispering of Mademoiselle Bourienne snapped her out of her daze. She looked up and, two steps away, saw Anatole with his arms around the Frenchwoman, whispering something to her. With a look of horror on his handsome face, Anatole glanced at Princess Mary but didn't immediately remove his arm from Mademoiselle Bourienne's waist — she hadn't yet noticed the princess.

"Who's that? Why? Wait a moment!" Anatole's face seemed to say. Princess Mary stared at them in silence. She couldn't make sense of it. Finally Mademoiselle Bourienne let out a scream and ran off. Anatole bowed to Princess Mary with a cheerful smile, as if inviting her to laugh at this strange scene, then shrugged his shoulders and walked toward the door leading to his own rooms.

An hour later, Tikhon came to summon Princess Mary to the old prince, adding that Prince Vasili was there too. When Tikhon arrived, Princess Mary was sitting on the sofa in her room, holding the weeping Mademoiselle Bourienne in her arms and gently stroking her hair. The princess's beautiful eyes, with all their former calm radiance, looked at Mademoiselle Bourienne's pretty face with tender affection and pity.
"No, Princess, I've lost your love forever!" said Mademoiselle Bourienne.
"Why? I love you more than ever," said Princess Mary, "and I will try to do everything I can for your happiness."
"But you must despise me. You, who are so pure, can never understand being swept away by passion. Oh, my poor mother..."
"I understand completely," Princess Mary answered with a sad smile. "Calm yourself, dear. I'll go to my father." And she went out.

Prince Vasili was sitting there with one leg thrown high over the other, a snuffbox in his hand, wearing a smile of deep emotion on his face, as if moved to his very core yet laughing at his own sentimentality. When Princess Mary entered, he hurriedly took a pinch of snuff.

"Ah, my dear, my dear!" he began, rising and taking both her hands. Then, sighing, he added: "My son's fate is in your hands. Decide, my dear, good, gentle Marie, whom I have always loved as a daughter!"
He stepped back, and a real tear appeared in his eye.

"Hmph... hmph..." Prince Bolkonski snorted. "The prince here is making you a proposal on behalf of his pupil — I mean, his son. Do you or do you not wish to become the wife of Prince Anatole Kuragin? Answer: yes or no," he shouted, "and then I reserve the right to state my opinion as well. Yes, my opinion, and only my opinion," he added, turning to Prince Vasili in response to his imploring look. "Yes or no?"
"My wish is never to leave you, Father — never to separate my life from yours. I don't want to marry," she answered firmly, looking at Prince Vasili and then at her father with her beautiful eyes.

"Nonsense! Rubbish! Nonsense, nonsense, nonsense!" Prince Bolkonski cried, frowning and seizing his daughter's hand. He didn't kiss it but simply pressed his forehead against hers and squeezed her hand so hard that she winced and let out a small cry.
Prince Vasili stood up.

"My dear, I must tell you that this is a moment I will never, never forget. But, my dear, won't you give us even a small hope of touching that kind and generous heart? Say 'perhaps'... The future is so long. Say 'perhaps.'"
"Prince, what I have said is everything in my heart. I thank you for the honor, but I will never be your son's wife."

"Well, that settles it, my dear fellow! I'm very glad to have seen you. Very glad! Go back to your rooms, Princess. Go!" said the old prince. "Very, very glad to have seen you," he repeated, embracing Prince Vasili.

"My calling is different," thought Princess Mary. "My calling is to find happiness of another kind — the happiness of love and self-sacrifice. Whatever it costs me, I will arrange poor Amelie's happiness. She loves him so passionately, and she repents so deeply. I will do everything I can to bring about their marriage. If he isn't rich, I'll give her the money. I'll ask my father and Andrew. I'll be so happy when she becomes his wife. She is so unfortunate — a stranger, alone, helpless! And, oh God, how passionately she must love him to have forgotten herself so completely! Perhaps I might have done the same!..." thought Princess Mary.

chapters.title: Book Three (1805) — Chapter 6
paragraphs: It had been a long time since the Rostovs had any news from Nicholas. It wasn't until the middle of winter that the count was finally handed a letter in his son's handwriting. He grabbed it and hurried to his study on tiptoe, anxious and excited, trying not to be noticed. He shut the door and began to read.

Anna Mikhaylovna, who always knew everything that went on in the house, heard about the letter's arrival and quietly slipped into the room. She found the count holding the letter, sobbing and laughing at the same time.
Anna Mikhaylovna's circumstances had improved, but she was still living with the Rostovs.
"My dear friend?" she said in a tone of sympathetic concern, ready to respond to whatever emotion was called for.
The count sobbed even harder.
"Nikolenka... a letter... he w-was... wounded... my dear boy... the countess... promoted to officer... thank God... How do I tell the countess!"

Anna Mikhaylovna sat down beside him, wiped the tears from his eyes and from the letter with her own handkerchief, then dried her own eyes, comforted the count, and came up with a plan: at dinner and through teatime she would prepare the countess, and after tea, with God's help, she would break the news.

At dinner, Anna Mikhaylovna talked constantly about war news and about Nikolenka, twice asking when the last letter from him had arrived — though she already knew. She kept hinting that they might very well receive a letter from him that day. Each time these hints made the countess anxious — she would glance uneasily at the count and at Anna Mikhaylovna — Anna Mikhaylovna deftly steered the conversation to some trivial topic. Natasha, who had the sharpest instincts of anyone in the family for detecting shifts in tone, expression, and mood, had been alert since the start of the meal. She was certain there was some secret between her father and Anna Mikhaylovna, that it had something to do with her brother, and that Anna Mikhaylovna was laying the groundwork. Bold as she was, Natasha knew how sensitive her mother was about anything involving Nikolenka and didn't dare ask questions at the table. But she was too excited to eat and kept squirming in her chair, ignoring her governess's reprimands. After dinner she rushed after Anna Mikhaylovna and, catching up in the sitting room, threw herself on her neck.
"Auntie, darling, please tell me what it is!"
"It's nothing, my dear."
"No, dearest, sweetest, honey — I won't give up. I know you know something."
Anna Mikhaylovna shook her head.
"You little sneak," she said.
"A letter from Nikolenka! I'm sure of it!" Natasha exclaimed, reading the confirmation in Anna Mikhaylovna's face.
"But for God's sake, be careful — you know how it could affect your mother."
"I will, I will, just tell me! You won't? Then I'll go tell everyone right now."
Anna Mikhaylovna gave her a brief summary of the letter's contents, on the condition that she tell no one.
"No, I swear on my honor," said Natasha, crossing herself, "I won't tell anyone!" And she immediately ran off to find Sonya.
"Nikolenka... wounded... a letter," she announced in gleeful triumph.
"Nicholas!" was all Sonya managed, instantly turning white.
Seeing the impact the news of her brother's wound had on Sonya, Natasha felt for the first time the painful side of it.
She threw her arms around Sonya and began to cry.
"It's just a small wound, but he's been made an officer. He's fine now — he wrote the letter himself," she said through her tears.

"There, you see! All you women are such crybabies," said Petya, striding around the room with large, determined steps. "I'm very glad, very glad indeed, that my brother has distinguished himself. You're all blubberers who don't understand anything."
Natasha smiled through her tears.
"Have you read the letter?" Sonya asked.
"No, but she said it's all over and that he's an officer now."
"Thank God!" said Sonya, crossing herself. "But maybe she wasn't telling the truth. Let's go to Mama."
Petya paced the room in silence for a moment.
"If I'd been in Nikolenka's place, I would have killed even more of those Frenchmen," he said. "What awful brutes they are! I would have killed so many there'd have been a pile of them."
"Be quiet, Petya — you're being ridiculous!"
"I'm not ridiculous — it's the people who cry over nothing who are ridiculous," Petya retorted.
"Do you remember him?" Natasha asked suddenly, after a moment of silence.
Sonya smiled.
"Do I remember Nicholas?"

"No, Sonya, what I mean is — do you remember him so well that you can picture him perfectly, everything about him?" Natasha said with an emphatic gesture, clearly trying to give her words a very specific meaning. "I remember Nikolenka too — I remember him well. But I don't remember Boris. Not at all."
"What! You don't remember Boris?" Sonya asked in surprise.

"It's not that I don't remember — I know what he looks like, but not the way I remember Nikolenka. With him, I just close my eyes and he's there. But Boris..." She shut her eyes. "No! Nothing at all."

"Oh, Natasha!" said Sonya, gazing at her friend with an intensity and seriousness that suggested she was saying something too important for jokes, almost as if speaking to someone else entirely. "I am in love with your brother, once and for all, and whatever may happen to him or to me, I will never stop loving him as long as I live."

Natasha looked at Sonya with curious, wondering eyes and said nothing. She felt that Sonya was telling the truth, that such love existed. But Natasha had never felt anything like it herself. She believed it was possible, but she didn't understand it.
"Will you write to him?" she asked.

Sonya grew thoughtful. The question of how to write to Nicholas, and whether she even should, tormented her. Now that he was an officer and a wounded hero, would it be right to remind him of her existence and of the promises he'd made?
"I don't know. I think if he writes to me, I'll write back," she said, blushing.
"And you wouldn't feel embarrassed writing to him?"
Sonya smiled.
"No."
"Well, I'd be embarrassed to write to Boris. I'm not going to."
"Why would you be embarrassed?"
"I don't know. It's just awkward. It would make me feel strange."

"I know why she'd be embarrassed," said Petya, still stinging from Natasha's earlier remark. "It's because she was in love with that fat one in glasses" — that was how Petya described his namesake, the new Count Bezukhov — "and now she's in love with that singer" — meaning Natasha's Italian singing teacher. "That's why she's embarrassed!"
"Petya, you're an idiot!" said Natasha.
"No more of an idiot than you, madam," said the nine-year-old Petya, with the air of a seasoned brigadier.

The countess had been prepared by Anna Mikhaylovna's hints at dinner. After retiring to her room, she sat in an armchair with her eyes fixed on a miniature portrait of her son on the lid of a snuffbox, tears steadily filling her eyes. Anna Mikhaylovna came tiptoeing to the countess's door with the letter and paused.
"Don't come in," she said to the old count, who was following her. "Come later." She went in and closed the door behind her.
The count pressed his ear to the keyhole and listened.

At first he heard the murmur of ordinary conversation, then Anna Mikhaylovna's voice alone in a long speech, then a cry, then silence, then both voices together in happy tones, and finally footsteps. Anna Mikhaylovna opened the door. Her face wore the proud expression of a surgeon who has just performed a difficult operation and is now allowing the audience to admire his skill.

"It's done!" she said to the count, gesturing triumphantly toward the countess, who sat holding the snuffbox with the portrait in one hand and the letter in the other, pressing them alternately to her lips.

When the countess saw the count, she stretched her arms out to him, embraced his bald head, and — looking past it at the letter and portrait — gently pushed it aside so she could press them to her lips once more. Vera, Natasha, Sonya, and Petya came into the room, and the reading of the letter began. After a brief description of the campaign and the two battles he'd fought in, along with his promotion, Nicholas wrote that he kissed his father's and mother's hands and asked for their blessing. He sent his love to Vera, Natasha, and Petya. He also sent greetings to Monsieur Schelling, Madame Schoss, and his old nanny, and asked them to kiss "dear Sonya, whom he loved and thought of just as always." When Sonya heard this, she blushed so deeply that tears sprang to her eyes and, unable to bear everyone's stares, she ran into the ballroom, spun around at full speed with her skirt billowing out like a balloon, and then, flushed and smiling, collapsed onto the floor. The countess was crying.
"Why are you crying, Mama?" Vera asked. "From everything he says, we should be happy, not crying."
This was perfectly true, but the count, the countess, and Natasha all looked at her reproachfully. "Who does she take after?" the countess thought.

Nicholas's letter was read hundreds of times, and anyone deemed worthy of hearing it had to come to the countess — she wouldn't let it out of her hands. The tutors came, and the nannies, and Dmitri, and several acquaintances, and each time the countess reread the letter with renewed pleasure, discovering fresh evidence of Nikolenka's virtues. How strange, how extraordinary, how wonderful it seemed that her son — the boy whose tiny movements she had felt inside her twenty years ago, the son she used to argue about with the overly indulgent count, the son who had first learned to say "pear" and then "granny" — that this son was now far away in a foreign land among strangers, a real man doing a man's work on his own, without help or guidance. The universal human experience, showing that children grow up gradually from cradle to adulthood, simply didn't exist for the countess. Every stage of her son's development had seemed just as miraculous to her as if no other child in history had ever grown up the same way. Just as it had once seemed impossible that the tiny creature living beneath her heart would ever cry, nurse at her breast, and learn to speak, so now she couldn't believe that little creature had become this strong, brave man, this model son and officer that his letter revealed him to be.

"What a style! How beautifully he describes things!" she said, reading the descriptive passages. "And what a soul! Not a word about himself... not a word! Something about some Denisov or other, though I'm sure he himself is braver than all of them. He says nothing about his own suffering. What a heart! How typical of him! And he remembered everyone! Didn't forget a single person. I always said, even when he was only this tall — I always said..."

For more than a week, preparations went on: drafts of letters to Nicholas from every member of the household were written and recopied, and under the countess's supervision and the count's careful attention, money and everything needed for the newly commissioned officer's uniform and equipment were gathered together. Anna Mikhaylovna, practical woman that she was, had even used her connections in the military to arrange an efficient way to send mail for herself and her son. She had access to a courier service going to Grand Duke Constantine Pavlovich, who commanded the Guards. The Rostovs assumed that "The Russian Guards, Abroad" was a perfectly adequate address, and that if a letter reached the Grand Duke commanding the Guards, there was no reason it couldn't be forwarded to the Pavlograd regiment, which was presumably somewhere nearby. So they decided to send the letters and money via the Grand Duke's courier to Boris, who would forward them to Nicholas. The letters came from the old count, the countess, Petya, Vera, Natasha, and Sonya, along with six thousand rubles for his outfitting and various other things the count sent his son.
